literal: By nature he was pure and frugal and did not pursue estates.
idiomatic: He was by nature frugal and did not amass property.

literal: With the Prince of Zhongshan Xi and his younger brother the Prince of Linhuai Yu and others, all were famed in the world for talent, learning, and commanding esteem.
idiomatic: He, Prince of Zhongshan Xi, and his younger brother Prince of Linhuai Yu were among those whose learning and reputation shone across the age.

literal: Though in graceful ease and ready wit he did not match Xi and Yu, in investigating antiquity and plain earnestness he surpassed them.
idiomatic: He lacked Xi and Yu's easy brilliance, but in scholarship and sober depth he outpaced them.

literal: Before long he was transferred to Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Soon he was made palace attendant.

literal: An edict ordered him together with Palace Attendant Cui Guang to compile and fix ritual garb regulations.
idiomatic: He was ordered with Palace Attendant Cui Guang to draft court dress rules.

literal: Later he also held the concurrent post of Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He later served concurrently as right vice director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: Because Yanming was broadly learned and widely informed, he was commanded to oversee metal and stone inscriptions.
idiomatic: His wide learning earned him charge of epigraphic and bell-cauldron matters.

literal: When Yuan Faseng rebelled, an edict made him Eastern-Route Mobile Secretariat, Grand Commander of Xuzhou, and controller of all military affairs, to campaign against Faseng together with Commander-in-Chief the Prince of Linhuai Yu, Minister of the Masters of Writing Li Xian, and others.
idiomatic: When Yuan Faseng rebelled, he was named eastern-route mobile secretariat and grand commander of Xuzhou, with command of all armies, and marched with Prince of Linhuai Yu, Minister Li Xian, and others against Faseng.

literal: Xiao Yan sent his Prince of Yuzhang Zong to garrison Xuzhou.
idiomatic: Xiao Yan posted his Prince of Yuzhang, Zong, to hold Xuzhou.

literal: Yanming had earlier governed the Xu region and won great praise among the people; he now rallied the old domain, and near and far submitted to him.
idiomatic: Having once governed Xu with a strong popular name, he called back the old land and won submission from far and near.

literal: Once Zong had surrendered, Yanming thereupon drove the army in pursuit, recovered the southeastern territory, and returned on reaching Suyu.
idiomatic: When Zong surrendered, Yanming pressed the pursuit, recovered the southeast as far as Suyu, and withdrew.

literal: He was transferred to Commander-in-Chief and Inspector of Xuzhou.
idiomatic: He was made commander-in-chief and inspector of Xuzhou.

literal: The region had repeatedly suffered armies; people and goods were wasted and ruined; Yanming rallied new settlers and old residents alike, so that all settled into their trades and the common folk all attached themselves to him.
idiomatic: War had repeatedly ravaged the region; he gathered old and new inhabitants until every household had its livelihood and the people clung to him.

literal: Under Emperor Zhuang he concurrently held Minister of the Masters of Writing and Grand Marshal.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Zhuang he served concurrently as director of the Masters of Writing and grand marshal.

literal: When Yuan Hao entered Luoyang, Yanming received Hao's trust, led troops, and held Heqiao Bridge.
idiomatic: When Yuan Hao took Luoyang, Yanming was entrusted with his cause and held Heqiao with an army.

literal: When Hao was defeated, he took wife and children and fled to Xiao Yan, and died in the lands south of the Yangzi.
idiomatic: Hao's fall sent him south to Xiao Yan with his family; he died in Jiangnan.

literal: At the end of Emperor Zhuang's reign his remains were returned.
idiomatic: Late in Zhuangdi's reign his coffin came home.

literal: At the beginning of the Deposed Emperor's reign he was posthumously given Grand Mentor, his princedom unchanged, posthumous title Wenzuan.
idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne he was posthumously titled grand mentor, his princedom left as before, with the temple name Prince Wenzuan.

literal: Works he authored—poems, fu, encomia, hymns, inscriptions, and dirges—numbered more than three hundred pieces; he also compiled Summaries of the Five Classics' Main Points and Separate Meanings of the Odes and Rites, and annotated Huangfu Mi's Chronological Record of Emperors and Kings and the Biographies of Transcendents.
idiomatic: He left more than three hundred poems, fu, hymns, inscriptions, and dirges, compiled Summaries of the Five Classics and Separate Meanings of the Odes and Rites, and annotated the Chronological Record of Emperors and Kings and the Biographies of Transcendents.

literal: Moreover, because Xin Du Fang of Hejian was skilled in calculation and astronomy, he brought him into his household academy.
idiomatic: He also summoned Xin Du Fang of Hejian, a master of mathematics, to his library.

literal: He compiled nine chapters and twelve diagrams on music old and new, and also gathered nine chapters on instrument standards; Fang separately annotated them, and all circulated in the world.
idiomatic: His nine chapters and twelve diagrams on music through the ages, and nine chapters on instrument measures with Fang's separate commentary, all circulated.

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: In the table of contents of all editions of Wei shu juan 20 this scroll is marked "lacuna"; after the scroll there should have been Song-dynasty collation notes, lost in transmitted copies.
idiomatic: Every Wei shu juan 20 table of contents marks this scroll "lacuna"; Song collation notes after the scroll are missing from transmitted copies.

literal: The Palace Edition textual verification states: "Wei Shou's book is lacunose here; later men supplemented it.
idiomatic: The Palace Edition notes: "Wei Shou's text is missing; later hands supplied this.

literal: " On examination the transmitted text, apart from a few words and phrases, matches Beishi juan 19, Biographies of Wenzong's Five Princes.
idiomatic: " The received text, save a few phrases, matches Beishi juan 19 (Wenzong's Five Princes).

literal: "Empress Xiaoyuan bore Emperor Xianwen": juan 13, Empresses and Consorts, has only "Empress Yuan" as posthumous title for Wenzong's Empress Yuan; juan 83 upper, Biography of Li Jun of the maternal kin,
idiomatic: "Empress Xiaoyuan bore Emperor Xianwen": in juan 13 she is posthumous "Empress Yuan" only; juan 83 upper, Li Jun of the maternal kin,

literal: 〈supplement〉
idiomatic: supplement

literal: and the supplement to juan 89, Biography of Li Hongzhi the Cruel Official, also speak only of "Empress Yuan"; only Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Hao's consort Lady Li Yuanchiang,
idiomatic: and the juan 89 supplement on the cruel official Li Hongzhi likewise say only "Empress Yuan"; only Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Hao's consort Lady Li Yuanchiang,

literal: 〈plate 183〉
idiomatic: plate 183

literal: calls her "Empress Yuangong," but the style "Xiaoyuan" is nowhere seen; "Xiao" is suspected to be a corruption of "Li."
idiomatic: titles her "Empress Yuangong," yet no "Xiaoyuan" title appears; "Xiao" likely corrupts "Li."

literal: "Quan with Li Ping, Gao Zhi, and others attacked and burned from four sides": Zhang Senkai's Beishi collation notes state: "Biography of Gao Zhao"
idiomatic: "Quan, Li Ping, Gao Zhi, and others attacked and burned from four sides": Zhang Senkai's Beishi collation reads "Biography of Gao Zhao"

literal: 〈Wei shu juan 83 lower, supplied from Beishi juan 80〉
idiomatic: Wei shu juan 83 lower (supplied from Beishi juan 80)

literal: has "Zhi" with the plant graph for "Zhi" with the multiply graph.
idiomatic: The text reads the plant-graph Zhi where the multiply-graph Zhi is meant.

literal: Commentary: The biography calls Gao Zhi, as inspector of Jizhou, "led provincial troops to defeat Yuan Yu, with separate-command merit," clearly the same man as this "Gao Zhi" with the multiply graph.
idiomatic: Note: Gao Zhi as Jizhou inspector "led provincial troops to defeat Yuan Yu with merit as detached commander"—clearly this Gao Zhi with the multiply graph.

literal: At the time it was customary for personal and place names often to interchange homophonic characters, but here it should be a graphic corruption of "Zhi" with the plant graph.
idiomatic: Homophones in names were common then, but here the plant-graph Zhi is clearly wrong.

literal: "Gao Cong and others of the Secretariat discussed and said": in various editions "Cong" is written "Min."
idiomatic: "Secretariat attendant Gao Cong and others submitted": editions read Cong as Min (clever graph).

literal: Beishi juan 19, Biographies of Wenzong's Five Princes; Cefu juan 580
idiomatic: Beishi juan 19 (Wenzong Five Princes); Cefu juan 580

literal: 〈folio 6957〉
idiomatic: folio 6957

literal: read "Cong."
idiomatic: have "Cong."

literal: Commentary: juan 68, Biography of Gao Cong, states that in the Taihe era he rose from Secretariat academician to attendant; at the time there was no such person as "Gao Min"; "Min" is corrupt and is now emended accordingly.
idiomatic: Note: juan 68 (Gao Cong) has him promoted from secretariat doctor to attendant in Taihe; no "Gao Min" then existed—Min is corrupt and the text is emended.

literal: "His son Lingdao succeeded, died, posthumous title Prince Dao": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Huan
idiomatic: "Son Lingdao inherited, died, titled Prince Dao": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan Huan

literal: 〈plate 161, no. 2〉
idiomatic: plate 161, no. 2

literal: has "Lingzun" for "Lingdao"; here the character "dao" should be a near-form corruption of "zun."
idiomatic: reads Lingzun for Lingdao; dao here is a near-graph corruption of zun.

literal: Moreover "Prince Dao" is "Prince Ai"; posthumous titles on epitaphs not only often differ from histories but differ epitaph to epitaph—not necessarily a biography error.
idiomatic: "Prince Dao" appears as "Prince Ai" on epitaphs; posthumous titles often diverge from histories and from stone to stone—not necessarily a biographical error.

literal: "His son You, styled Bosou": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan You has "shou" with the hand-over graph written "yuan" with the aid graph; "shou" is suspected corrupt.
idiomatic: "Son You, courtesy name Bosou": Muzhi jishi, epitaph of Yuan You reads shou as yuan; shou is likely corrupt.
